paragraphs: 54 submitted Multiple sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in regulation of T cell activation (GO:0050863).

Among the co-stimulatory molecules enriched in this term, CD28 functions as a prototypical activating receptor on T cells that lowers the threshold for T cell receptor signalling when engaged by its ligands. In Multiple sclerosis, genetic and functional studies implicate altered CD28-mediated co-stimulation in shaping pathogenic effector T cell responses within the central nervous system, consistent with a skewing of the balance between tolerance and autoimmunity. The ligands CD80 and CD86, expressed on antigen-presenting cells, provide the cognate signals to CD28 and thereby influence the intensity and duration of T cell activation in Multiple sclerosis lesions and peripheral immune compartments.

The inhibitory co-receptor cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA4) is a high-affinity binder of CD80 and CD86 and dampens T cell activation by competing with CD28 and recruiting inhibitory signalling machinery. Variants and functional alterations in CTLA4 have been linked to susceptibility and disease course in Multiple sclerosis, supporting a role for impaired negative regulation of T cell activation in this disease. Programmed cell death protein 1 (PDCD1) and its ligand CD274 provide an additional inhibitory axis that constrains chronically stimulated T cells, and perturbation of this pathway has been associated with exacerbation of central nervous system autoimmunity in Multiple sclerosis.

The interleukin-2 receptor alpha chain IL2RA is enriched in this pathway and forms the high-affinity receptor complex for the cytokine IL2 together with IL2RG, transducing signals via downstream kinases and transcription factors. In Multiple sclerosis, genetic variation and altered expression of IL2RA are consistently implicated in disease susceptibility and in the balance between regulatory and effector T cell populations, indicating that dysregulated IL2–IL2RA signalling contributes to defective immune tolerance. IL2 itself promotes clonal expansion and survival of activated T cells but is also crucial for regulatory T cell homeostasis, so alterations in IL2 signalling represented by IL2 and IL2RA in this pathway are highly relevant to the failure to contain autoreactive T cells in Multiple sclerosis.

Signal transducer and activator of transcription proteins STAT5A and STAT5B, which are activated downstream of IL2RA- and IL2RG-containing receptor complexes, are central transcriptional effectors of cytokine-driven T cell differentiation and survival. In the context of Multiple sclerosis, aberrant activation of a cytokine-responsive transcription factor-dependent transcriptional programmes favours the persistence of pro-inflammatory T cell subsets at the expense of regulatory populations, further linking cytokine receptor signalling in this enriched pathway to disease pathogenesis. Transforming growth factor beta 1 (TGFB1), another key cytokine in this intersection, provides a counter-regulatory signal that can promote regulatory T cell differentiation and limit effector T cell activation, and disruptions in TGFB1-mediated regulation have been associated with heightened neuroinflammation in Multiple sclerosis.

Interleukin-6 (IL6), represented in this term together with its signalling component IL6ST, is a pleiotropic cytokine that promotes T cell activation and differentiation toward pathogenic effector phenotypes under inflammatory conditions. In Multiple sclerosis, elevated IL6 signalling has been related to enhanced T cell-driven neuroinflammation and lesion formation, aligning the enrichment of IL6 and IL6ST in this pathway with a shift toward sustained T cell activation. The common gamma-chain cytokine receptor subunit IL2RG, shared by multiple cytokine receptors, further broadens the range of cytokine inputs that can modulate T cell activation states in Multiple sclerosis.

The pan-leukocyte phosphatase PTPRC is a critical regulator of proximal T cell receptor signalling by setting the phosphorylation state of key signalling components. In Multiple sclerosis, altered function or expression of PTPRC has been associated with changes in T cell activation thresholds and signalling quality, which can favour autoreactive T cell responses. Together with non-receptor phosphatases such as PTPN11, PTPN2 and PTPN22 in this enriched set, PTPRC highlights the importance of phosphatase-mediated fine-tuning of T cell activation in Multiple sclerosis.

Beyond these individually highlighted proteins, the remaining intersection proteins enriched in regulation of T cell activation segregate into several functional clusters. A T cell receptor signalling machinery cluster, including CD3E, FYN, LCK, ZAP70, LAT, VAV1, RAC2, RHOH, NCK1, NCK2, SOS1, SOS2, SYK, SRC, YES1 and LYN, comprises kinases, adaptors and small GTPase regulators that propagate and shape early T cell receptor signals. A co-stimulatory and co-inhibitory surface receptor cluster, including CD1D, CD2, CD27, CD5, CD69, CD83, CD274, CD80, CD86, SLAMF1 and HAVCR2, provides additional activating or inhibitory cues that calibrate T cell activation in tissue-specific contexts relevant to Multiple sclerosis. A cytokine and growth factor signalling cluster, comprising IL2, IL2RG, IL6, IL6ST, TGFB1, EPO, IGF1, IGF2, KITLG, JAK2, JAK3, STAT5A and STAT5B, links extracellular cytokine and growth factor availability to transcriptional programmes governing T cell proliferation, survival and differentiation. Finally, a regulatory phosphatase and scaffold cluster containing PTPRC, PTPN11, PTPN2, PTPN22, LGALS3, SDC4, EFNB1, EFNB2, EFNB3 and RHOA integrates phosphatase activity with adhesion and cytoskeletal dynamics, thereby modulating the strength, duration and spatial organisation of T cell activation signals in Multiple sclerosis lesions.

Overall, enrichment of 54 Multiple sclerosis associated proteins in the term “regulation of T cell activation” underscores that dysregulated control of T cell activation is a central feature of Multiple sclerosis immunopathology. Co-stimulatory and co-inhibitory checkpoints such as CD28 and CTLA4, together with the high-affinity IL2 receptor component IL2RA, appear to drive the association by linking genetic and functional evidence for altered T cell activation thresholds directly to this pathway. Well-documented interactions within this enriched set, including binding of CD28 and CTLA4 to CD80 and CD86, engagement of PDCD1 by its ligand CD274, and signalling from IL2 through IL2RA–IL2RG to STAT5A and STAT5B, illustrate how coordinated perturbations across receptors, ligands and downstream signalling modules can converge to sustain pathogenic T cell responses in Multiple sclerosis. These findings support the view that therapeutic strategies targeting the regulation of T cell activation at multiple levels may be particularly effective in modifying disease activity in Multiple sclerosis.

paragraphs: Exactly 41 Multiple sclerosis associated proteins were significantly enriched in the GO:BP pathway “positive regulation of T cell activation” (GO:0050870).

Among the proximal T cell receptor signaling molecules enriched in this term, PTPN22, LCK and ZAP70 stand out as key regulators of T cell activation thresholds. PTPN22 encodes a lymphoid protein tyrosine phosphatase that constrains antigen receptor signaling, and genetic variation in PTPN22 has been repeatedly linked to altered T cell reactivity in Multiple sclerosis, consistent with a role in skewing the balance toward pathogenic activation. LCK, a Src family kinase, and the ζ‑chain–associated kinase ZAP70 form a critical tandem at the T cell receptor complex, where LCK-mediated phosphorylation events enable ZAP70 activation; perturbations in this axis have been implicated in abnormal T cell signaling profiles described in Multiple sclerosis, supporting their contribution to excessive or dysregulated positive regulation of T cell activation in the disease context.

A second group of notable proteins comprises HAVCR2, SLAMF1 and TGFB1, which modulate the quality and persistence of T cell activation in inflammatory settings. HAVCR2 functions as an inhibitory receptor on T cells that is often upregulated in chronically stimulated lymphocytes, and altered HAVCR2 expression patterns have been reported in Multiple sclerosis, suggesting maladapted attempts to restrain ongoing T cell activation. SLAMF1, an immunoglobulin superfamily receptor involved in co-stimulatory signaling, is expressed on activated T cells and has been found upregulated in Multiple sclerosis lesions, consistent with its participation in sustaining pathogenic T cell responses within the central nervous system. TGFB1, a pleiotropic cytokine with well-established roles in T cell differentiation and activation control, shows genetic and expression-level alterations in Multiple sclerosis that are compatible with disturbed regulatory circuits governing the intensity and duration of T cell activation.

The remaining proteins enriched in this term can be organized into functional clusters centered on co-stimulation, cytokine and growth factor signaling, and intracellular signal transduction. A co-stimulatory and antigen-recognition cluster includes CD1D, CD27, CD28, CD3E, CD5, CD80, CD83, CD86, CD274, SLAMF1 and HAVCR2, which collectively provide additional signals beyond T cell receptor ligation to enhance or shape T cell activation, and several of these molecules have been implicated in Multiple sclerosis through altered expression on peripheral or lesional T cells and antigen-presenting cells. A cytokine and growth factor cluster, incorporating IL2, IL2RA, IL2RG, IL6, IL6ST, EPO, IGF1, IGF2, KITLG and TGFB1, supports the expansion, survival and differentiation of activated T cells through receptor-mediated positive regulation of activation programs, and dysregulation of these pathways has been observed in Multiple sclerosis immune compartments. Finally, an intracellular signaling and cytoskeletal-remodeling cluster, including FYN, LYN, SRC, YES1, SYK, VAV1, JAK2, STAT5B, PTPN11, NCK1, NCK2, RHOA, RHOH and PTPRC, integrates signals from the T cell receptor, co-stimulatory receptors and cytokine receptors to propagate and stabilize activation, with several members reported to show altered activation states or expression in Multiple sclerosis T cells, consistent with globally enhanced positive regulation of T cell activation.

Taken together, enrichment of these proteins in “positive regulation of T cell activation” underscores that a core feature of the Multiple sclerosis gene module is the reinforcement of signaling pathways that drive and sustain T cell activation. The association appears to be driven particularly by proximal T cell receptor regulators such as PTPN22, LCK and ZAP70, whose combined disruption can substantially alter activation thresholds. Well-documented interactions among the proteins listed for this record, including the functional pairing of LCK and ZAP70 at the T cell receptor complex and the engagement of CD28 by its co-stimulatory ligands CD80 and CD86, highlight that multiple, physically connected signaling nodes are concurrently represented. This convergence supports the interpretation that the Multiple sclerosis module is enriched for an interconnected network of molecules that together amplify the positive regulation of T cell activation.

paragraphs: 27 submitted Multiple sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in T cell receptor signaling pathway (GO:0050852).

Among the phosphatases enriched in this term, PTPN22 and PTPN2 stand out as central regulators of proximal T cell receptor signaling with strong relevance to Multiple sclerosis. PTPN22 encodes a cytoplasmic tyrosine phosphatase that dampens early T cell receptor signaling by dephosphorylating key activating motifs, and genetic variation in PTPN22 is one of the most consistently replicated risk factors for autoimmune demyelination, indicating that altered tuning of T cell activation thresholds contributes to disease susceptibility. PTPN2 is a non-receptor tyrosine phosphatase that constrains cytokine and T cell receptor–driven pathways; Multiple sclerosis studies have implicated PTPN2 through genetic association and through altered expression in immune cells, supporting a role in limiting pathogenic T cell responses within this pathway. ZAP70, a kinase that binds phosphorylated a cluster-of-differentiation 3 marker chains and propagates the initial signal from the engaged receptor, is also enriched here, and defects or dysregulation of ZAP70-dependent signaling have been linked to abnormal T cell activation profiles in Multiple sclerosis, consistent with its position as a proximal amplifier of antigen recognition.

Several lipid-signaling enzymes in this pathway further connect T cell receptor signaling strength to Multiple sclerosis. BTK, a Tec-family kinase best known in B cells but also expressed in myeloid and some T cell subsets, participates in transducing signals downstream of immune receptors, and pharmacologic BTK inhibition has shown clinical activity in Multiple sclerosis, underscoring the importance of BTK-dependent signaling nodes in modulating neuroinflammation. PIK3CD encodes the p110δ catalytic subunit of phosphoinositide 3-kinase, which generates phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphates in response to receptor engagement; enhanced or prolonged PIK3CD activity has been associated with aberrant survival and effector differentiation of lymphocytes in Multiple sclerosis, aligning with its role in sustaining T cell receptor–driven activation. INPP5D, a 5′-inositol phosphatase that antagonizes phosphoinositide 3-kinase products, limits downstream Akt and calcium signaling, and decreased INPP5D function or expression in immune cells from people with Multiple sclerosis has been linked to exaggerated activation states, suggesting that imbalance between PIK3CD and INPP5D within this pathway may favor pathogenic T cell responses.

Effector and cytotoxic T cell–related molecules enriched in this term further support a role for T cell receptor signaling in Multiple sclerosis lesion biology. LGALS3 encodes galectin-3, a carbohydrate-binding protein that modulates immune synapse organization and receptor clustering; it is upregulated in active Multiple sclerosis lesions, and experimental data indicate that galectin-3 can potentiate T cell receptor signaling and inflammatory cytokine production, providing a bridge between extracellular matrix remodeling and intracellular signal amplification. CD8A and CD8B, the coreceptor chains defining major cytotoxic T cell subsets, facilitate recruitment of proximal kinases to the engaged receptor complex; clonally expanded a cluster-of-differentiation 8 marker-positive T cells are a hallmark of Multiple sclerosis lesions, and enrichment of CD8A and CD8B in this pathway is consistent with a prominent contribution of cytotoxic T cell receptor engagement to tissue damage in the disease.

The remaining proteins enriched in this term organize into several functional clusters that together constitute the canonical T cell receptor signaling apparatus. A co-receptor and core-complex cluster (CD247, CD3E, CD28, CD8A, CD8B) assembles and stabilizes the receptor at the T cell surface and provides costimulatory input that shapes the quality of the downstream response. A proximal tyrosine kinase cluster (LCK, FYN, ITK, TEC, TXK, ZAP70) transduces receptor and co-receptor engagement into widespread phosphorylation of downstream substrates, thereby controlling the amplitude and duration of signaling. An adaptor and scaffold cluster (LAT, LCP2, FYB1, NCK1, CRKL, SH2D1A, LGALS3) nucleates multiprotein complexes at the activated receptor, coordinating inputs to diverse effector pathways including cytoskeletal rearrangement and transcriptional activation. A phosphoinositide and calcium-signaling cluster (PIK3CD, PLCG1, PLCG2, INPP5D) integrates receptor engagement with generation and turnover of lipid second messengers and inositol trisphosphate, linking the T cell receptor to calcium flux and metabolic adaptation. Finally, a regulatory and structural immune cell cluster (PTPN2, PTPRC) sets basal signaling thresholds and maintains T cell identity by modulating the phosphorylation state of proximal components and defining leukocyte-specific signaling environments.

Overall, enrichment of these proteins in the T cell receptor signaling pathway indicates that multiple layers of antigen-receptor signaling control, from proximal phosphorylation events to lipid-mediated amplification and phosphatase-mediated restraint, are recurrently perturbed in Multiple sclerosis. Within this network, PTPN22, BTK and CTLA4 are the proteins that most strongly drive the association, because of their central regulatory roles and established involvement in disease-modifying signaling at the T cell receptor. Well-characterized interactions such as the recruitment and activation of ZAP70 by phosphorylated CD247, and the coupling of LAT with LCP2 to assemble downstream signaling complexes, illustrate how coordinated function of the proteins listed for this record shapes T cell responses that can either promote or limit demyelinating pathology. Together, these findings support the view that fine-tuning of T cell receptor signaling is a critical determinant of Multiple sclerosis risk and course, and highlight multiple nodes within this pathway as potential targets for therapeutic modulation.

paragraphs: 50 submitted Multiple sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in regulation of leukocyte cell-cell adhesion (GO:1903037).

Among the adhesion regulators, ITGA4 is particularly notable, as it encodes the α4 integrin chain that mediates firm leukocyte attachment to vascular and stromal ligands and has been directly targeted in MS therapy to limit pathogenic leukocyte trafficking into the central nervous system. In MS lesions, ITGA4-dependent adhesive interactions help sustain leukocyte clustering and retention at the blood–brain barrier, and the enrichment of ITGA4 in this pathway underscores the central role of modulated integrin-mediated cell-cell contacts in disease. Within the same adhesive axis, LGALS3, a β-galactoside-binding lectin expressed by immune and endothelial cells, can bind integrins and other surface glycoproteins to stabilize or reorganize adhesive junctions, and has been detected in inflammatory CNS lesions in MS, linking galectin-dependent lattice formation to dysregulated leukocyte adhesion in the inflamed brain. TGFB1, a pleiotropic cytokine with well-established immunoregulatory roles in MS, also modulates integrin activation states and the adhesive properties of T cells and myeloid cells, suggesting that altered TGFB1 signaling may fine-tune ITGA4- and LGALS3-dependent leukocyte aggregation at vascular and perivascular interfaces.

Proximal T cell receptor signaling molecules enriched in this term provide a second layer of control over leukocyte cell-cell adhesion. LCK, a Src-family tyrosine kinase, orchestrates early T cell receptor signaling events that rapidly convert antigen recognition into inside-out activation of integrins such as ITGA4, thereby controlling the strength and duration of T cell contacts with antigen-presenting cells; genetic and functional data have implicated LCK activity in shaping pathogenic T cell responses in MS. ZAP70, another key kinase in this cascade, depends on LCK-mediated phosphorylation for its recruitment and activation at the T cell receptor complex, and has been linked to MS through its role in promoting stable immune synapse formation between autoreactive T cells and antigen-presenting cells in the CNS and peripheral lymphoid tissues. PTPRC (a cluster-of-differentiation 45 marker), a leukocyte-specific phosphatase that regulates the activation thresholds of LCK and other kinases, is widely expressed on MS-relevant lymphocyte and myeloid subsets and modulates both the initiation and maintenance of adhesive immune synapses in the CNS compartment.

a cytokine-associated kinase–a cytokine-responsive transcription factor signaling components enriched in this pathway connect cytokine responses to the regulation of leukocyte adhesion in MS. JAK2 and JAK3, non-receptor tyrosine kinases activated downstream of multiple cytokine receptors, have been implicated in MS by virtue of their roles in promoting expansion and survival of pro-inflammatory lymphocyte subsets that display enhanced integrin-dependent adhesion and tissue infiltration. STAT5A and STAT5B, transcription factors activated by JAK2 and JAK3, contribute to the differentiation and persistence of cytokine-driven effector and regulatory T cell populations in MS, partly by controlling expression of adhesion-related molecules and chemokine receptors that govern cell-cell contact patterns. PTPN22, a cytoplasmic phosphatase with strong genetic association to autoimmune disease including MS, negatively regulates antigen receptor signaling and thereby influences the propensity of autoreactive T and B cells to form and stabilize adhesive contacts with antigen-presenting cells in both peripheral lymphoid organs and the CNS.

The remaining proteins enriched in this term can be organized into functional clusters that together shape the regulation of leukocyte cell-cell adhesion. paragraphs: 7 submitted Multiple sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in protein tyrosine phosphatase activity (GO:0004725).

Within this set, PTPRC, PTPN22 and PTPN2 stand out as central immune regulators whose molecular functions map directly onto pathogenic mechanisms in Multiple sclerosis. PTPRC encodes the receptor-type phosphatase a cluster-of-differentiation 45 marker, a prototypic protein tyrosine phosphatase that dephosphorylates key signaling residues on antigen receptor–associated kinases in lymphocytes, thereby tuning the threshold for T cell and B cell activation; genetic and functional alterations in a cluster-of-differentiation 45 marker have repeatedly been linked to aberrant lymphocyte signaling in Multiple sclerosis. PTPN22 encodes a cytoplasmic protein tyrosine phosphatase that dephosphorylates components of the T cell receptor and innate immune signaling machinery; a well-characterized autoimmunity-associated missense variant in PTPN22 has been implicated in susceptibility to Multiple sclerosis, consistent with its capacity to reshape effector and regulatory T cell responses. PTPN2, another non-receptor phosphatase, operates on cytokine receptor and antigen receptor pathways, including those driven by inflammatory cytokines, and has been associated with autoimmune phenotypes that overlap with the immune dysregulation observed in Multiple sclerosis.

PTK2, PTPN11 and PTPN12 connect protein tyrosine phosphatase activity to adhesion-dependent and cytokine-dependent signaling circuits that are relevant to central nervous system immune infiltration in Multiple sclerosis. PTK2 encodes focal adhesion kinase, a non-receptor tyrosine kinase that is functionally intertwined with phosphatases in this pathway: it becomes phosphorylated in response to integrin engagement and growth factor stimulation, promoting cell adhesion, migration and survival of immune cells and glia that participate in lesion formation. PTPN11 encodes the a non-intersection pathway component phosphatase, which dephosphorylates and thereby modulates signaling intermediates downstream of multiple receptors, including the interleukin-6-type cytokine receptors discussed in the literature on principles of interleukin-6-type cytokine signalling; by shaping interleukin-6 family cytokine responses, a non-intersection pathway component influences inflammatory cascades that are active in Multiple sclerosis. PTPN12 is a cytoplasmic phosphatase that directly targets focal adhesion components such as PTK2, acting as a negative regulator of adhesion and motility signaling, and thus has the potential to restrain the migratory behavior of immune cells that infiltrate the central nervous system in Multiple sclerosis.

The remaining proteins can be grouped into clusters based on their shared regulatory roles at the cell surface and within cytoplasmic signaling complexes. One cluster comprises the receptor-type phosphatase PTPRK, which, as highlighted in recent work revisiting protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type kappa, localizes to sites of cell–cell contact where it dephosphorylates adhesion and junctional components; through this activity, PTPRK is positioned to influence tissue organization and barrier properties that are perturbed in the inflamed Multiple sclerosis central nervous system. A second cluster includes the broadly acting cytoplasmic phosphatases PTPN11, PTPN12 and PTPN2, which share the ability to dephosphorylate multiple receptor-proximal substrates and thereby integrate signals from cytokine receptors, antigen receptors and adhesion molecules into coherent cellular responses in immune and glial cells.

Taken together, enrichment of these proteins in the protein tyrosine phosphatase activity pathway indicates that control of tyrosine dephosphorylation, and its balance with kinase activity, is a prominent feature of the Multiple sclerosis gene module. The association appears to be driven largely by immune signaling phosphatases such as PTPRC and PTPN22, together with the closely coupled kinase PTK2, which anchor this pathway in antigen receptor and adhesion signaling that are critical for pathogenic lymphocyte activation and trafficking. Within the intersection, PTPN12 is known to directly dephosphorylate PTK2, illustrating how phosphatases and kinases in this set form an interconnected network that fine-tunes adhesion-dependent signaling. These coordinated activities support a model in which dysregulated protein tyrosine phosphatase activity contributes to the aberrant immune activation and central nervous system infiltration characteristic of Multiple sclerosis.

paragraphs: Exactly 10 Multiple sclerosis associated proteins were significantly enriched in the cytokine receptor activity pathway (GO:0004896).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, IL2RA, IL2RB and IL2RG form the high‑affinity interleukin‑2 receptor complex, which binds IL‑2 and transduces signals that are essential for T cell proliferation and regulatory T cell homeostasis. In Multiple sclerosis, nitration of this receptor complex has been shown to limit regulatory T cell expansion and function, with the study of IL‑2R nitration directly implicating impairment of IL2RA-, IL2RB- and IL2RG‑mediated signaling in aggravating disease pathogenesis, placing this trimeric receptor at the center of the cytokine receptor activity enrichment.

IL6R and IL6ST together constitute the signaling componentry for IL‑6‑type cytokines, with IL6R conferring ligand binding and IL6ST acting as the common signal‑transducing subunit. In the context of Multiple sclerosis, IL‑6–dependent pathways are closely linked to pathogenic effector T cell and B cell responses, so the joint enrichment of IL6R and IL6ST within cytokine receptor activity underscores the importance of IL‑6 family receptor signaling in shaping the inflammatory milieu. GHR, as the receptor for growth hormone, also signals through overlapping downstream pathways and has been implicated in modulating neuroinflammation and tissue repair, suggesting that altered GHR‑mediated cytokine receptor activity may influence the balance between damage and recovery in the central nervous system.

The remaining proteins enriched in this pathway segregate into two functional clusters characterized by distinct cytokine receptor activities. A myeloid growth factor receptor cluster comprises CSF2RB, IL5RA and FLT3, all of which transmit signals from hematopoietic cytokines to regulate proliferation, survival and functional polarization of myeloid and progenitor populations that participate in Multiple sclerosis lesion formation and resolution. A tissue‑protective cytokine receptor cluster includes EPOR together with GHR, IL6R and IL6ST, reflecting receptors whose activation in neural and glial compartments can modulate cell survival, oxidative stress responses and inflammatory signaling within the central nervous system.

Overall, enrichment of these 10 proteins in cytokine receptor activity highlights that aberrant reception and transduction of cytokine signals is a central molecular function in Multiple sclerosis. The strongest contribution to this signal is provided by the IL‑2 receptor subunits IL2RA, IL2RB and IL2RG, whose post‑translational modification and impaired signaling directly exacerbate disease in experimental and clinical settings. Coordinated signaling through IL6R–IL6ST and the myeloid‑oriented receptors CSF2RB, IL5RA and FLT3 further emphasizes that both lymphoid and myeloid cytokine pathways converge on this molecular function. Well‑documented physical and functional interactions within the IL‑2 receptor trimer (IL2RA–IL2RB–IL2RG) and within the IL‑6 receptor complex (IL6R–IL6ST) exemplify how multimeric cytokine receptors integrate extracellular cues into the pathogenic immune responses that characterize Multiple sclerosis.

paragraphs: 12 submitted Multiple sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in immune receptor activity (GO:0140375).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, the interleukin-2 receptor subunits IL2RA, IL2RB, and IL2RG exemplify immune receptor activity most clearly, forming the high-affinity receptor complex that transduces interleukin-2-dependent signals in T cells. Genetic and immunological studies have consistently linked IL2RA to Multiple sclerosis susceptibility, and the broader literature on abnormal a cluster-of-differentiation 4 marker T cell activation and cytotoxic a cluster-of-differentiation 4 marker T cell expansion in Multiple sclerosis underscores the relevance of dysregulated interleukin-2 receptor signaling in maintaining or amplifying autoreactive T cell pools. IL2RB and IL2RG, as the signal-transducing components of this receptor, likely act as principal molecular effectors of this pathway in the disease by coupling ligand engagement at the cell surface to downstream activation cascades in brain-homing, autoreactive a cluster-of-differentiation 4 marker T cells that are sustained by chronic immune receptor stimulation.

A second notable group within this pathway consists of the cytokine receptors IL6R and IL6ST together with the shared beta-chain CSF2RB. IL6R and the transducing subunit IL6ST form the functional receptor complex for interleukin-6, a cytokine implicated in myeloid and lymphoid activation during neuroinflammation, aligning with observations that myeloid-cell mediated neuroinflammation is an important component of Multiple sclerosis pathology. CSF2RB serves as a common beta subunit for several hematopoietic cytokine receptors that drive proliferation and activation of myeloid lineage cells, providing a mechanistic link between immune receptor engagement, microglial and myeloid activation, and processes such as myelin debris clearance and remyelination described in experimental models of Multiple sclerosis.

The remaining enriched proteins can be organized into two functional clusters of immune receptors. An Fc receptor cluster comprising FCGR2A and FCGR3A mediates recognition of IgG-opsonized targets, thereby coupling immune complexes to activating signals in myeloid and B-lineage cells that contribute to B cell–driven neuroinflammation and the activation of autoreactive T cells. A hematopoietic and growth factor receptor cluster including FLT3, EPOR, GHR, and IL5RA encompasses receptors that govern survival and differentiation of hematopoietic and effector cell subsets; through their shared function as ligand-activated transmembrane receptors, they provide additional routes by which peripheral immune activation states can shape the composition and responsiveness of the cellular populations that participate in Multiple sclerosis lesions.

Together, the enrichment of these 12 proteins in immune receptor activity (GO:0140375) highlights that a substantial fraction of the Multiple sclerosis module is dedicated to sensing extracellular immune cues and converting them into intracellular activation in T cells, B cells, and myeloid cells. IL2RA, IL2RG, and IL6R emerge as key drivers of this association because they are central signaling receptors in pathways directly implicated in autoreactive a cluster-of-differentiation 4 marker T cell activation and chronic neuroinflammation. The physical and functional interactions among these proteins, such as the assembly of IL2RA, IL2RB, and IL2RG into the high-affinity interleukin-2 receptor and the pairing of IL6R with IL6ST to form the interleukin-6 receptor complex, illustrate how multiple enriched subunits cooperate to amplify immune receptor signaling in Multiple sclerosis.

paragraphs: 14 submitted Multiple sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in immunological synapse (GO:0001772).

Among the enriched proteins, CD28, CD3E and ZAP70 exemplify molecules that are integral to T‑cell receptor signal initiation at the immunological synapse. CD3E is a structural constituent of the T‑cell receptor–a cluster-of-differentiation 3 marker complex embedded in the synaptic membrane, and thereby provides part of the scaffold on which signaling complexes assemble in Multiple sclerosis lesions. CD28, revisited here in its synaptic context, resides at the central supramolecular activation cluster where it delivers co‑stimulatory signals that modulate T‑cell activation thresholds in Multiple sclerosis. ZAP70 is a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase that is rapidly recruited to phosphorylated a cluster-of-differentiation 3 marker chains at the synapse; altered ZAP70-dependent signaling has been implicated in shaping the balance between pathogenic and regulatory T‑cell responses in Multiple sclerosis.

Cytotoxic effector function within the immunological synapse is represented by PRF1, GZMA and GZMB, which localize to secretory granules that polarize toward the synaptic cleft during lymphocyte–target cell contact. PRF1 forms pores in the target cell membrane, providing a conduit through which the serine proteases GZMA and GZMB can enter and induce cell death; dysregulation of this granule exocytosis machinery has been linked to aberrant cytotoxic activity in Multiple sclerosis tissue. HAVCR2, already introduced in earlier pathways, localizes to the synaptic membrane as an inhibitory receptor that can dampen T‑cell effector function, and changes in its expression or engagement at the immunological synapse have been associated with disease activity in Multiple sclerosis.

A second group of enriched proteins consists of signaling adaptors, kinases and GTPase regulators that transiently accumulate at the immunological synapse rather than forming its permanent structural core. LAT serves as a membrane-tethered adaptor in the synaptic signaling microclusters, where it nucleates multi‑protein complexes downstream of the T‑cell receptor. LCK is a Src-family tyrosine kinase that localizes to the inner leaflet of the synaptic membrane, where it phosphorylates a cluster-of-differentiation 3 marker chains and co‑receptors to initiate signal propagation. VAV3, RHOH and ARHGDIA are regulators of Rho-family GTPases that are recruited to the synapse to coordinate actin remodeling and microcluster dynamics, processes that influence the stability and organization of the immunological synapse in Multiple sclerosis.

Additional proteins enriched in this term highlight adhesive and lectin-mediated aspects of synapse organization. ALCAM is a cell adhesion molecule that contributes to the physical apposition of lymphocytes with their target cells at the synaptic interface, while LGALS3 (galectin‑3) can accumulate in the perisynaptic area where it modulates receptor clustering and lattice formation on the cell surface. Together with the more signaling‑focused proteins, these molecules underscore that the immunological synapse is a discrete subcellular compartment in which structural components (such as CD3E, LAT and ALCAM) and transient residents (such as LCK, ZAP70, VAV3, PRF1, GZMA and GZMB) co‑localize; however, such co‑localization alone does not constitute evidence that they act through a single shared mechanism in Multiple sclerosis.

Overall, enrichment of these 14 proteins in the immunological synapse component suggests that a substantial fraction of the Multiple sclerosis gene module converges on the specialized junction where lymphocytes recognize and potentially damage target cells. The association is driven in particular by CD28, PRF1 and ZAP70, which respectively represent co‑stimulatory signaling, granule-mediated cytotoxicity and T‑cell receptor signal transduction at the synapse. Well‑characterized interactions between intersection proteins, such as LCK-mediated phosphorylation of CD3E leading to ZAP70 recruitment, and PRF1-dependent delivery of GZMB into target cells, reinforce the notion that perturbations in synapse assembly and function are central to the immunopathology of Multiple sclerosis. These findings emphasize that the relevant disease biology occurs at a defined cell–cell contact site rather than being uniformly distributed across the lymphocyte surface or cytoplasm.

paragraphs: 55 submitted Multiple sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in receptor complex (GO:0043235).

Within this enriched set, IL2RA, IL2RB and IL2RG exemplify cytokine receptor subunits that assemble into multimeric receptor complexes at the lymphocyte surface, where they bind interleukin-2 and initiate intracellular signaling. Their enrichment in the receptor complex term underscores that MS genetic risk and immunopathology converge on the composition and signaling competence of these membrane receptor assemblies rather than on isolated signaling enzymes, consistent with evidence that altered interleukin-2 receptor complex formation modifies T cell function in MS.

The enrichment of IL6, IL6R and IL6ST points to a similar focus on the IL6 receptor complex, which is composed of ligand-binding and signal-transducing subunits and is central to pro‑inflammatory signaling in MS lesions. In this context, these proteins are not acting as generic cytokines or adaptors but as defined components of a membrane receptor complex whose abundance and configuration influence how glial cells and infiltrating leukocytes respond to inflammatory cues in MS.

Adhesion-related receptor complexes are also prominent in the intersection, particularly ITGA4, ITGB1 and ALCAM, which form part of heterodimeric integrin and immunoglobulin-like receptor complexes at the cell surface. In MS, these complexes are critical at the level of the blood–brain barrier, where their engagement regulates firm adhesion and transmigration of pathogenic lymphocytes into the central nervous system, making the localization of these molecules to receptor complexes directly relevant to lesion formation.

Several neurotrophic and growth factor receptor complexes are represented by NTRK1, NTRK2 and EPHA2, together with ERBB3 and ERBB4, which function as receptor tyrosine kinases on neurons and glial cells. In MS and its models, these receptors participate in complexes that can promote or limit axonal damage and remyelination depending on ligand availability and co-receptor context, highlighting that the disease involves not only immune receptor complexes but also neuroglial receptor assemblies that shape tissue repair capacity.

Metabolic and growth-related receptor complexes are captured by the enrichment of IGF1R, GHR, INSR and the signaling adaptor IRS1, which reside in hormone and growth factor receptor complexes at the plasma membrane and, upon activation, in endosomal compartments. Experimental work in MS models indicates that such complexes influence oligodendrocyte survival and myelin maintenance, so their co-localization within receptor complexes emphasizes a compartmentalized regulation of neuroglial resilience in the disease.

The receptor complex term from the GO cellular component ontology specifies where these proteins localize—principally to multi-subunit receptor assemblies at the plasma membrane and, in some cases, associated endosomal or intracellular receptor complexes—rather than what they do biochemically. Many of the enriched proteins, such as IL2RB, IL6R, CSF2RB, CD247, CD3E, CD79A, CD79B, CD8A, CD8B, EPHA2, ERBB3, ERBB4, FGFR1–FGFR4, FLT3, FLT4, GHR, IGF1R, INSR, an integrin-alpha subunit and a non-intersection pathway component family members, KDR, KIT, MET, NTRK1, NTRK2, PDGFRA, PDGFRB, RET, TEK and TGFBR3, form structural components of receptor complexes, typically spanning the membrane and providing ligand-binding and dimerization interfaces. Others, including JAK1, JAK2, LYN, SYK, ZAP70, PTK2B, IRS1 and LRP1, are more transient residents that associate with the cytoplasmic tails of these receptors upon activation to propagate downstream signals. While co-enrichment of these proteins in the receptor complex compartment supports the idea that MS risk and pathology are concentrated in membrane signaling hubs, co-localization alone is not evidence of a single shared mechanism across all of these receptors.

Beyond the individually highlighted proteins, the remaining intersection proteins can be organized into functional clusters of receptor complexes. A first cluster comprises cytokine receptor–a cytokine-associated kinase signaling complexes, including IL2RB, IL2RG, IL5RA, IL6, IL6ST, CSF2, CSF2RB, JAK1 and JAK2, which assemble at the cell surface to bind cytokines and couple them to a cytokine-associated kinase-mediated phosphorylation cascades. A second cluster consists of antigen receptor signalosomes, formed by CD247, CD3E, CD79A, CD79B, CD8A, CD8B, ZAP70, LYN and SYK, which co-localize in T and B cell receptor complexes at the immunological synapse to initiate antigen-dependent activation. A third cluster encompasses receptor tyrosine kinase complexes dedicated to growth and guidance, including EPHA2, ERBB3, ERBB4, FGFR1–FGFR4, FLT3, FLT4, GHR, IGF1R, INSR, IRS1, KDR, KIT, MET, NTRK1, NTRK2, PDGFRA, PDGFRB, RET, TEK and TGFBR3, which form multimeric complexes that transduce developmental, angiogenic and neurotrophic signals. Finally, adhesion and matrix-interaction receptor complexes are represented by ALCAM, ITGA1, ITGA2, ITGA3, ITGA5, ITGB1, ITGB4, ITGB5, ITGB8, LRP1 and PTK2B, which assemble at cell–cell and cell–matrix contact sites to regulate leukocyte trafficking and tissue organization in MS lesions.

Taken together, enrichment of 55 MS-associated proteins in the receptor complex cellular component term indicates that a substantial fraction of MS genetic and molecular risk is concentrated in multi-subunit receptor assemblies that orchestrate immune activation, leukocyte trafficking, vascular remodeling and neuroglial survival. Within this term, IL2RA, IL6R and ITGA4 appear to be key drivers, reflecting convergent evidence on cytokine receptor and adhesion receptor complexes in MS. Well-documented interactions among the intersection proteins, such as the formation of the IL6–IL6R–IL6ST complex, the heterotrimeric IL2RA–IL2RB–IL2RG receptor complex with associated a cytokine-associated kinase kinases, the T cell receptor complex incorporating CD247, CD3E and ZAP70, the B cell receptor complex containing CD79A and CD79B with SYK and LYN, and the ITGA4–ITGB1 integrin heterodimer, illustrate that these proteins operate in tightly organized receptor structures. This pathway therefore refines the view of MS pathogenesis by emphasizing that disease-relevant signaling is compartmentalized within specific receptor complexes rather than being uniformly distributed across the cell surface or cytosol.

paragraphs: 53 submitted Multiple sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in external side of plasma membrane (GO:0009897).

The proteins enriched in this term are united by their localization to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane, where they are embedded as transmembrane receptors or adhesion molecules, anchored via extracellular domains, or transiently bound as ligands. In this context, canonical B‑cell surface components such as CD19, CD79A, CD79B and FCRL2 highlight the external side of the plasma membrane of B lymphocytes as a prominent compartment in Multiple sclerosis, consistent with studies implicating B‑cell receptor signaling and age‑associated B cells in disease, including work on B cell‑intrinsic IL‑2 signaling and IL‑10–producing a cluster-of-differentiation 25 marker‑positive subsets. Co‑localization in this compartment does not in itself demonstrate a shared mechanism, but it emphasizes that these B‑cell–restricted markers and signaling adaptors are structurally positioned to integrate antigen recognition and cytokine cues at the cell surface in Multiple sclerosis–relevant immune infiltrates.

A second notable group comprises cell‑surface molecules that directly control leukocyte trafficking across the blood–brain and blood–CSF barriers. ITGA4 and ITGB1 form a heterodimeric integrin at the external side of the plasma membrane that mediates firm adhesion of lymphocytes to endothelial ligands during transendothelial migration, a process closely scrutinized in Multiple sclerosis and in related central nervous system inflammatory conditions characterized by chemokine‑driven cell entry. SELL and PECAM1, likewise enriched in this compartment, participate in leukocyte rolling and diapedesis at the luminal endothelial surface, underlining that the external plasma membrane of circulating and endothelial cells is a key anatomical site at which pathological immune cell recruitment into the central nervous system is orchestrated in Multiple sclerosis.

A third set of externally oriented immune checkpoints and co‑stimulatory receptors further underscores the functional specialization of this membrane leaflet in tuning adaptive immunity in Multiple sclerosis. PDCD1 resides at the outer plasma membrane of activated T and B cells where it engages its ligand CD274, which is also enriched here, to dampen effector responses; the same surface hosts CD28 and CTLA4, which bind CD80 and CD86 on antigen‑presenting cells, as well as CD27 and SLAMF1, all of which occupy the external side of the plasma membrane as part of immunological synapses in cerebrospinal fluid and lesion‑infiltrating lymphocytes. Although these molecules were introduced in earlier pathways, their shared enrichment in this compartment specifically emphasizes that the disease‑relevant balance between activation, co‑stimulation and inhibition is physically organized at the external face of the plasma membrane in Multiple sclerosis.

The remaining enriched proteins can be organized into functional clusters that further characterize this compartment. A cytokine and growth‑factor receptor cluster includes CSF2RB, IL5RA, IL6R, IL6ST, EPOR, GHR, INSR, KDR, PDGFRA and TGFBR3, which together mark the external side of the plasma membrane as a hub for receiving hematopoietic growth factors, interleukins and trophic signals implicated in immunomodulatory oligodendrocyte biology and central nervous system inflammation. A cell‑adhesion and immunoglobulin‑superfamily cluster, including ALCAM, CD1B, CD1C, CD1D, CD2, CD3E, CD5, CD8A, CD9, SDC1, PECAM1 and THBS1, reflects stable structural constituents of the external leaflet that mediate antigen presentation, cell–cell contact and matrix interaction at sites of demyelinating pathology. A cluster of Fc and complement‑related receptors and effector molecules, represented by FCGR2A, FCGR3A and PLG, marks the capacity of the external membrane to bind immune complexes and proteolytic regulators in antibody‑driven inflammation. Finally, apoptosis‑ and activation‑linked surface proteins such as FASLG, CD69, CD83 and SELL indicate that the external side of the plasma membrane is also a platform for regulating cell survival and activation status in Multiple sclerosis lesions and cerebrospinal fluid, even though their co‑localization here does not prove a single shared pathogenic mechanism.

Taken together, enrichment of these 53 proteins in the external side of plasma membrane term suggests that key Multiple sclerosis processes converge on the outer leaflet of immune and vascular cell membranes as a critical anatomical site for B‑cell signaling, leukocyte trafficking and immune checkpoint engagement. Within this compartment, CD19, ITGA4 and PDCD1 appear to drive the association by linking B‑cell identity, integrin‑mediated central nervous system entry and inhibitory receptor signaling, respectively. Well‑documented interactions among the enriched proteins, such as the formation of the ITGA4–ITGB1 integrin heterodimer and the binding of PDCD1 to CD274 or CD28 and CTLA4 to CD80 and CD86, illustrate how multiple surface molecules positioned on the external side of the plasma membrane can cooperate to modulate immune cell behavior in Multiple sclerosis, even though the enrichment analysis itself does not resolve the directionality or magnitude of these effects. Co‑localization in this cellular compartment therefore highlights, but does not on its own establish, shared mechanisms of disease among the listed proteins.

paragraphs: 19 submitted Multiple sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Th17 cell differentiation (KEGG:04659).

Within this pathway, IL2, IL6 and TGFB1 represent key upstream cytokine drivers of Th17 cell differentiation that are repeatedly implicated in Multiple sclerosis. IL2, together with its role in Th17 biology highlighted by the observation that interferon-beta can inhibit Th17 cell differentiation in patients with Multiple sclerosis, is positioned on the KEGG map as an initiating ligand feeding into downstream signaling that constrains or promotes Th17 lineage decisions. IL6, which is central to the concept of Th17 cell pathogenicity in autoimmune disease, occupies a parallel upstream ligand position and, in the context of Multiple sclerosis, provides a cytokine milieu that favors differentiation toward inflammatory Th17 phenotypes, in line with experimental data showing that modulation of Th17 differentiation can ameliorate disease. TGFB1, also enriched in this pathway, is mapped as a cooperating cytokine that shapes Th17 development and is consistent with data indicating that myelin antigen–driven Th17 responses can be induced even in healthy individuals and are enhanced in patients with Multiple sclerosis, underscoring a TGFB1- and IL6-dependent permissive environment for pathogenic Th17 cells.

On the KEGG Th17 cell differentiation map, the enriched proteins span the canonical cytokine–receptor–a cytokine-associated kinase–a cytokine-responsive transcription factor axis, with IL2RA, IL2RB and IL2RG forming the IL2 receptor complex downstream of IL2, and IL6R and IL6ST constituting the corresponding receptor module downstream of IL6. These receptors converge on JAK1, JAK2 and JAK3, which are represented as proximal tyrosine kinases that transmit signals from the IL2 and IL6 receptor complexes into the nucleus via STAT5A and STAT5B. In the context of Multiple sclerosis, the literature on interferon-beta–mediated inhibition of Th17 differentiation and on pharmacological modulation of Th17 cells is consistent with this receptor–a cytokine-associated kinase–a cytokine-responsive transcription factor axis being a modifiable hub that determines the balance between pathogenic and less pathogenic Th17 subsets.

A second segment of the Th17 cell differentiation pathway enriched in this analysis involves proximal T cell signaling components that provide the activating scaffold for Th17 lineage commitment. CD247 and CD3E, which here are considered specifically in their role within the Th17 pathway rather than their broader functions, lie at the membrane-proximal end of the map and couple antigen recognition to downstream signaling. Immediately downstream, LCK, ZAP70 and LAT form a contiguous block on the KEGG map, relaying activation signals that are required for efficient Th17 differentiation. PLCG1, positioned further along this branch, links these proximal events to calcium-dependent and transcriptional programs that have been experimentally tied to the generation of pathogenic Th17 cells in autoimmune settings, including Multiple sclerosis.

Taken together, the remaining enriched proteins can be organized into three functional clusters that complete the Th17 differentiation module. A cytokine receptor cluster comprising IL2RA, IL2RB, IL2RG, IL6R and IL6ST encompasses the membrane components that translate IL2 and IL6 availability into intracellular signaling potential. A a cytokine-associated kinase–a cytokine-responsive transcription factor signal transduction cluster, including JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, STAT5A and STAT5B, forms the core of the downstream phosphorylation and transcriptional machinery that integrates inputs from these receptors during Th17 lineage specification. Finally, a T cell activation signalosome cluster, consisting of CD247, CD3E, LAT, LCK, ZAP70 and PLCG1, provides the antigen-dependent co-stimulatory context that cooperates with cytokine signals to drive Th17 cell differentiation and pathogenicity.

Overall, enrichment of these 19 proteins in Th17 cell differentiation supports a central contribution of this pathway to Multiple sclerosis pathogenesis, consistent with experimental data showing that both pharmacological modulation and endogenous regulators can alter Th17-mediated disease. The association appears to be driven principally by the upstream cytokines IL2, IL6 and TGFB1, which together define the inflammatory and differentiation milieu for Th17 cells in Multiple sclerosis. The proteins are concentrated along a largely contiguous branch of the KEGG map that links cytokine ligands and receptors through JAK1–JAK2–JAK3 to STAT5A–STAT5B, and further connects to the CD247–CD3E–LCK–ZAP70–LAT–PLCG1 signalosome, highlighting well-documented physical and functional interactions within this axis. This coordinated enrichment indicates that both cytokine-driven and antigen-driven components of Th17 cell differentiation are jointly perturbed in Multiple sclerosis.

paragraphs: 28 submitted Multiple sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in cytokine-receptor signal transduction signaling pathway (KEGG:04630).

Among the enriched proteins, JAK1, JAK2 and JAK3 occupy the central transducing tier of the KEGG cytokine-receptor signal transduction map, where they couple a wide range of cytokine and growth factor receptors to downstream transcriptional responses. Multiple studies of neuroinflammatory disease, including Multiple sclerosis, have implicated dysregulated a cytokine-associated kinase activity in both innate and adaptive immune compartments, and the supplied literature specifically links aberrant a cytokine-associated kinase/a cytokine-responsive transcription factor signaling to T-cell modulation in the Multiple sclerosis brain and to innate immune activation in neuroinflammatory lesions. Consistent with this, pharmacological modulation of the a cytokine-associated kinase/a cytokine-responsive transcription factor axis has been proposed as a therapeutic strategy in Multiple sclerosis, and the enrichment of all three a cytokine-associated kinase paralogues underscores that the core kinase module of this pathway is represented in the gene set.

STAT5A and STAT5B represent the canonical nuclear effectors for several of the enriched receptors, and their phosphorylation by JAK1–JAK3 is a key step in transcriptional programming downstream of cytokines such as IL2. The literature connecting a cytokine-associated kinase/a cytokine-responsive transcription factor and PPARγ signaling, as well as analyses of the a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme/Akt/mTOR–a cytokine-associated kinase/a cytokine-responsive transcription factor axis in Multiple sclerosis, implicate a cytokine-responsive transcription factor-dependent transcription in shaping pathogenic versus regulatory T-cell responses and in sustaining chronic inflammation. In this context, the simultaneous enrichment of IL2, IL2RA, IL2RB and IL2RG within the same pathway highlights that both the receptor complex and its principal a cytokine-responsive transcription factor effectors are represented, pointing to altered IL2–a cytokine-responsive transcription factor signaling as a plausible contributor to T-cell dysregulation in Multiple sclerosis.

The enrichment of PIK3CB and PIK3CD in this pathway captures the documented crosstalk between a cytokine-associated kinase/a cytokine-responsive transcription factor and a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme signaling that has been analyzed in detail in Multiple sclerosis. In the KEGG map, these kinases are recruited by activated cytokine and growth factor receptors, where they branch from the cytokine-receptor signal transduction core toward a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme/Akt/mTOR signaling, and the supplied literature emphasizes that this integrated axis shapes survival and effector functions of immune cells in Multiple sclerosis. PDGFB together with its receptors PDGFRA and PDGFRB lies at the growth factor end of the same module and can feed into both a cytokine-associated kinase/a cytokine-responsive transcription factor and a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-dependent cascades, suggesting that growth factor–driven remodeling of CNS-resident cells and infiltrating leukocytes intersects with the cytokine-driven a cytokine-associated kinase/a cytokine-responsive transcription factor circuitry highlighted by the enrichment.

Within the KEGG cytokine-receptor signal transduction pathway topology, the enriched proteins span from extracellular ligands and receptors, through membrane-proximal kinases and adaptors, to nuclear a cytokine-responsive transcription factor effectors, but they are most concentrated along the cytokine receptor–a cytokine-associated kinase–a cytokine-responsive transcription factor branch, with additional, partially contiguous extensions into a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme and Ras-related signaling nodes. CSF2, IL2, IL3, IL6 and PDGFB, together with their cognate receptors (CSF2RB, IL2RA, IL2RB, IL2RG, IL6R, IL6ST, PDGFRA, PDGFRB, EPOR and GHR), occupy the upstream ligand–receptor segment; JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, PIK3CB, PIK3CD, SOS1, SOS2, PTPN11 and PTPN2 form the intermediary transduction layer; and STAT5A and STAT5B reside at the downstream transcriptional output. Through PIK3CB and PIK3CD this branch connects directly to the adjacent KEGG a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme-Akt signaling map, while SOS1 and SOS2 provide entry points into Ras/a non-intersection pathway component maps, and the cytokine ligands and receptors themselves participate in the cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction map, emphasizing how the enriched proteins anchor cytokine-receptor signal transduction signaling within a broader signaling network that is also implicated in Multiple sclerosis by the supplied literature.

The remaining enriched proteins group into two main functional clusters. A cytokine and growth factor receptor cluster comprises CSF2 and its receptor subunit CSF2RB, EPO and EPOR, GHR, IL2 together with IL2RA and IL2RB and IL2RG, IL3, IL5RA, IL6 with its receptor IL6R and the shared signal transducer IL6ST, and PDGFB with PDGFRA and PDGFRB; collectively, this cluster represents the ligand–receptor interface that determines which immune and glial cell types feed into the cytokine-receptor signal transduction cascade. A second cluster contains PIK3CB, PIK3CD, SOS1, SOS2, PTPN11, PTPN2, JAK3 and STAT5A, which function as proximal kinases, adaptors and phosphatases that modulate signal strength and diversify outputs toward a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme and Ras effector pathways while refining a cytokine-responsive transcription factor-dependent transcription; this regulatory layer aligns with the described a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme/Akt/mTOR–a cytokine-associated kinase/a cytokine-responsive transcription factor crosstalk and innate immune control in Multiple sclerosis.

Overall, the enrichment of these 28 proteins in the cytokine-receptor signal transduction signaling pathway suggests that dysregulated cytokine and growth factor signaling, transmitted through a contiguous a cytokine-associated kinase–a cytokine-responsive transcription factor axis and its a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme and Ras branches, is a central feature of the Multiple sclerosis-related gene module. JAK1, JAK2 and STAT5B appear to drive this association, as they occupy pivotal positions linking multiple enriched receptors to transcriptional programs that have been implicated in Multiple sclerosis pathogenesis. Well-documented interactions among the enriched proteins include the recruitment and activation of JAK1–JAK3 by receptor complexes containing IL2RA, IL2RB and IL2RG, the subsequent phosphorylation and dimerization of STAT5A and STAT5B, and the modulation of these signals by PTPN2 and PTPN11 as well as by a phosphoinositide signalling enzyme isoforms and a guanine-nucleotide-exchange factor-family adaptors. Together, these interconnected nodes provide a coherent mechanistic framework for how convergent cytokine and growth factor inputs could sustain chronic neuroinflammation and immune dysregulation in Multiple sclerosis through the cytokine-receptor signal transduction pathway and its immediate network neighbors.

paragraphs: 15 submitted Multiple sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Th1 and Th2 cell differentiation (KEGG:04658).

Within this pathway, IL2 and its high-affinity receptor subunit IL2RA, previously noted in other contexts of this report, here mark the cytokine axis that directly shapes Th1 and Th2 polarization in Multiple sclerosis, in line with work highlighting altered Th1/Th2 balance in the disease. Their shared γ-chain partner IL2RG, which is enriched in this term alongside them, anchors the receptor complex that couples Th1/Th2-skewing cytokine exposure to downstream signaling, consistent with studies showing that pharmacologic modulation of T cell differentiation can ameliorate experimental and clinical Multiple sclerosis by shifting helper T cell subset composition.

Downstream of these receptors, JAK1, JAK2, JAK3 and the transcription factors STAT5A and STAT5B form a canonical a cytokine-associated kinase–a cytokine-responsive transcription factor module that transduces IL2-family signals into Th1- and Th2-polarizing transcriptional programs. The enrichment of these proteins in the Th1 and Th2 cell differentiation pathway, together with literature describing Th1/Th2 signature cytokines as central drivers of autoimmune inflammation in Multiple sclerosis, supports a model in which aberrant activation or regulation of this a cytokine-associated kinase–a cytokine-responsive transcription factor cassette contributes to the pathogenic helper T cell profiles observed in patients.

The T cell antigen receptor branch of the pathway is represented by CD247 and CD3E in the a cluster-of-differentiation 3 marker complex, together with the proximal tyrosine kinase LCK and the ZAP70–LAT signaling node. These proteins integrate antigen recognition with Th1/Th2 differentiation cues, and their enrichment is consistent with evidence that differences between mouse and human T cell biology, including in proximal the T-cell antigen receptor signaling, shape how Th1 and Th2 subsets contribute to Multiple sclerosis pathogenesis and response to immunomodulatory interventions.

The remaining enriched proteins cluster into two functional signaling modules. A the T-cell antigen receptor–a cluster-of-differentiation 3 marker signaling module comprises CD247, CD3E, LCK, ZAP70, LAT and the effector enzyme PLCG1, which together form a contiguous block on the KEGG map from the T-cell antigen receptor engagement through LAT- and PLCG1-dependent second-messenger generation; this module lies in the receptor-proximal and signal transduction segment of the Th1/Th2 pathway and cross-talks extensively with the KEGG T cell receptor signaling pathway. A common γ-chain cytokine receptor and a cytokine-associated kinase kinase module comprises IL2RB, IL2RG, JAK1, JAK2, JAK3 and STAT5A, which occupy the cytokine receptor and a cytokine-associated kinase–a cytokine-responsive transcription factor signaling arm of the map and provide a direct mechanistic link to the KEGG a cytokine-associated kinase–a cytokine-responsive transcription factor signaling and cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction pathways, thereby connecting extracellular Th1/Th2-polarizing cytokines to transcriptional effector outputs that are not themselves represented among the intersection proteins.

Overall, the enrichment of these 15 proteins in Th1 and Th2 cell differentiation underscores the central contribution of dysregulated helper T cell subset specification to Multiple sclerosis. The association appears to be driven primarily by IL2, IL2RA and STAT5B, which anchor the cytokine receptor and transcriptional effector ends of the IL2–a cytokine-associated kinase–a cytokine-responsive transcription factor axis that shapes Th1/Th2 fate decisions. On the KEGG map, the intersection proteins form a largely contiguous block spanning upstream IL2 family receptors through a cytokine-associated kinase–a cytokine-responsive transcription factor and the T-cell antigen receptor-proximal signaling, rather than distal lineage-defining transcription factors, highlighting signaling-level perturbations as a key feature. Consistent with this, well-documented interactions among the intersection proteins include IL2 binding to the IL2RA/IL2RB/IL2RG receptor complex, activation of JAK1 and JAK3 and subsequent phosphorylation of STAT5A and STAT5B, and cooperative signaling from CD247–CD3E through LCK, ZAP70, LAT and PLCG1 to integrate antigen recognition with cytokine-driven Th1/Th2 differentiation in Multiple sclerosis.

paragraphs: 25 submitted Multiple sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Leukocyte transendothelial migration (KEGG:04670).

Within this pathway, the integrin heterodimer components ITGA4 and ITGB1, together with the endothelial adhesion receptor PECAM1, represent key membrane-proximal determinants of leukocyte adhesion and diapedesis that are directly relevant to Multiple sclerosis. ITGA4–ITGB1 mediates firm arrest of circulating leukocytes on the vascular wall and their subsequent crawling along the endothelium, and blockade of ITGA4 is an established disease-modifying strategy in relapsing Multiple sclerosis, underscoring the centrality of this adhesion axis to pathogenic central nervous system entry. PECAM1 is concentrated at endothelial junctions where it supports leukocyte passage between endothelial cells; altered PECAM1 expression and function at the blood–brain barrier have been associated with inflammatory lesion formation in Multiple sclerosis, linking this junctional molecule to disease-related endothelial barrier dysfunction.

Immediately downstream of these adhesion receptors, the Rho-family GTPases RHOA, RAC2 and CDC42 integrate signals that reorganize the actin cytoskeleton and regulate formation of protrusive and contractile structures needed for transendothelial migration. In the leukocyte transendothelial migration map, these GTPases occupy a central signaling node between adhesion engagement and cytoskeletal effectors, and dysregulated RHOA- and RAC2-dependent contractility has been implicated in aberrant endothelial barrier control and immune cell motility in Multiple sclerosis and its experimental models. CDC42 contributes to cell polarity and directional migration; perturbations in CDC42-controlled polarity programs in immune cells have been linked to altered trafficking patterns in Multiple sclerosis, consistent with an imbalance between pathogenic and regulatory leukocyte subsets accessing the central nervous system.

A second signaling hub enriched in this pathway is formed by the phosphoinositide 3-kinase catalytic subunits PIK3CB and PIK3CD together with the phospholipase C isoforms PLCG1 and PLCG2, which lie along a contiguous branch of the KEGG map connecting integrin and immune-receptor engagement to downstream motility responses. PIK3CD is a dominant catalytic isoform in lymphocytes, and genetic and expression data from blood-derived signatures in Multiple sclerosis point to altered PIK3CD-driven signaling in patients, compatible with enhanced survival and trafficking competence of pathogenic leukocytes. PIK3CB participates in parallel phosphoinositide pathways that support endothelial cell responses to leukocyte adhesion, while PLCG1 and PLCG2 generate diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate to modulate calcium-dependent motility programs; both a phospholipase isoforms have been implicated in shaping immune cell activation thresholds and migration patterns in Multiple sclerosis cohorts.

Upstream of these enzymatic signaling nodes, the non-receptor tyrosine kinases ITK and TXK, together with the adaptor-like GTPase RHOH and the guanine nucleotide exchange factors VAV1, VAV2 and VAV3, connect antigen receptor and costimulatory cues to the Rho-family module within the leukocyte transendothelial migration pathway. These proteins occupy the receptor-proximal signaling segment of the KEGG map, where they feed into PIK3CB/PIK3CD and PLCG1/PLCG2 activation as well as RHOA, RAC2 and CDC42 loading. ITK and TXK have been linked to T cell polarization and effector differentiation in Multiple sclerosis, while VAV1 family members and RHOH have been implicated by genetic and transcriptional studies in disease susceptibility and severity, consistent with a scenario in which heightened receptor-proximal signaling lowers the threshold for pathogenic leukocyte activation and promotes their access to the inflamed central nervous system.

The remaining proteins enriched in this term fall into several functional clusters along the KEGG leukocyte transendothelial migration map. An integrin–focal adhesion scaffold cluster comprising PTK2, PTK2B, PXN, ACTN1, ACTN4 and AFDN links ITGA4–ITGB1 engagement to the actin cytoskeleton at adhesion sites; these proteins are also annotated in adjacent KEGG focal adhesion and regulation of actin cytoskeleton maps, highlighting cross-talk between leukocyte transendothelial migration and generic adhesion remodeling pathways. A cytoskeletal-regulatory GTPase cluster formed by ARHGAP35 together with the effector-associated GTPases RHOA, RAC2 and CDC42 connects receptor-proximal signals to local activation and inactivation cycles of Rho-family proteins that drive shape changes during diapedesis. A proximal signaling and phosphoinositide–calcium cluster including PTPN11, PIK3CB, PIK3CD, PLCG1 and PLCG2 integrates tyrosine phosphorylation with second-messenger production and is shared with adjacent KEGG immune-receptor signaling maps, reflecting direct cross-talk between leukocyte activation and migratory machinery. paragraphs: 68 submitted Multiple sclerosis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Cytokine Signaling in Immune system (REAC:R-HSA-1280215).

In the Reactome hierarchy this term sits as a cytokine-focused child pathway directly under the Immune System event, and many of the enriched proteins participate as components of cytokine receptor complexes or as their immediate catalytic partners. Within the IL2 receptor module, IL2RA and IL2RG, together with IL2, are annotated as structural components and ligand of the same multimeric receptor complex, whereas JAK1 and JAK3 act as associated catalytic tyrosine kinases on the cytoplasmic tails of these receptor subunits; these proteins therefore function within the same early reaction steps of receptor engagement and intracellular signal initiation. In Multiple sclerosis, genetic and immunological data implicate altered IL2–IL2 receptor signaling, and the enrichment of this complete receptor–kinase assembly suggests that dysregulated IL2-dependent pathways are a central axis of cytokine signaling perturbation in the disease.

A parallel architecture is evident for IL6 signaling, where IL6, IL6R and IL6ST form a ligand–receptor complex that is annotated as a single membrane-associated unit in Reactome, while JAK2 serves as a catalytic kinase bound to the receptor’s intracellular domains; these components again participate in the same proximal reaction steps that follow cytokine binding. In Multiple sclerosis, IL6-driven pathways have been linked to pathogenic effector T cell differentiation, and the concurrent enrichment of IL6, its receptor components and the associated JAK2 kinase underscores that the full IL6 signaling module, rather than isolated elements, is involved in disease-relevant cytokine networks.

Several enriched proteins act as intracellular negative regulators that are recruited to activated cytokine receptor complexes in successive signaling steps. SH2B3 is annotated as an adaptor that binds phosphorylated cytokine receptor–a cytokine-associated kinase complexes and modulates their activity, acting as a scaffold rather than a catalyst; variants in SH2B3 have been associated with altered susceptibility to Multiple sclerosis, consistent with a role in tuning cytokine responsiveness. PTPN2 is a catalytic tyrosine phosphatase that dephosphorylates JAKs and receptor tails downstream of their activation, and INPP5D is a lipid phosphatase that hydrolyses phosphoinositides generated by receptor-proximal kinases; both act in later reactions that follow the initial a cytokine-associated kinase-mediated phosphorylation events, and both have been implicated in the control of autoimmune inflammation in Multiple sclerosis–relevant immune cell populations.

Additional notable intracellular effectors link cytokine receptor activation to broader signaling cascades over successive steps. PTK2B functions as a catalytic non-receptor tyrosine kinase that is recruited to membrane complexes downstream of cytokine receptors and integrins, amplifying signals through phosphorylation of adaptor proteins, and genetic studies have associated PTK2B with Multiple sclerosis risk. PIK3CD and PLCG2 are catalytic enzymes that act on membrane phosphoinositides after their recruitment by phosphorylated receptor complexes and adaptor proteins such as CRK, CRKL and SHC1; PIK3CD generates phosphatidylinositol trisphosphates that propagate survival and differentiation signals, whereas PLCG2 hydrolyses phosphatidylinositol bisphosphates to produce second messengers, and perturbations in these pathways have been linked to aberrant lymphocyte activation in Multiple sclerosis.

The remaining enriched proteins in this pathway can be organized into several functional clusters. A first cluster comprises non-receptor tyrosine kinases and adaptor proteins that relay signals from engaged cytokine receptors, including JAK2, JAK3, FYN, LCK, LYN, SRC, HCK, CRK, CRKL, SHC1, GRAP2, GAB2, NCK1, SOS1, SOS2 and PTK2B; these act predominantly as catalysts or scaffold components within membrane-proximal signaling complexes. A second cluster encompasses phosphoinositide and metabolic signaling regulators downstream of cytokine receptors, including PIK3CB, PIK3CD, PLCG1, PLCG2, INPP5D, INPPL1, IRS1 and IRS2, which are annotated as catalytic enzymes or docking substrates in successive lipid and metabolic reaction steps. A third cluster contains cell-surface immune modulators and matrix/adhesion-related proteins, such as CD27, CD80, CD86, HAVCR2, SDC1, ITGB1, LAMA5 and COL1A2, which function as components of receptor or adhesion complexes that condition cytokine responses. A final cluster is formed by secreted cytokines, growth factors, their receptors and matrix-modifying effectors, including CSF2, CSF2RB, IL2, IL3, IL5RA, IL6, IL6R, FGF2, HGF, GHR, IGHG1, FASLG, FLT3, BLNK, CDC42, RHOU, HGF, MMP1, MMP2 and F13A1, which participate as ligands, receptor subunits, downstream GTPases or extracellular catalysts within the broader chain of cytokine-driven reactions.

Overall, enrichment of Cytokine Signaling in Immune system indicates that Multiple sclerosis risk and pathology converge on a densely connected set of cytokine receptor complexes and their immediate intracellular effectors. The association is driven most strongly by the coordinated presence of IL2RA, IL6ST and JAK1, which together anchor key receptor–kinase assemblies that initiate IL2- and IL6-family signaling. Well-documented interactions between intersection proteins, such as the formation of IL2–IL2RA–IL2RG–JAK1–JAK3 and IL6–IL6R–IL6ST–JAK2 complexes, and the downstream recruitment of adaptors including CRK, CRKL and SHC1, support a model in which perturbations at multiple successive steps of cytokine signaling collectively shape the inflammatory milieu in Multiple sclerosis. The pathway-level enrichment therefore highlights cytokine receptor modules and their proximal signal transducers as central mechanistic nodes through which genetic and immunological risk factors may exert their effects in the disease.
